Agent / contributor instructions for tflplanner

Source: AGENTS.md

This repository is the R package tflplanner (DESCRIPTION is at the root): a ‘shiny’ app and functions that manage clinical TFL studies on top of tflspec and rtfreporter. This file holds the rules for working on the code.

Read these first

Topic Document
How to contribute: issues, fork and pull request, the checks before a PR CONTRIBUTING.md
What the app is made of (studies, specs, screens) vignettes/articles/concepts.Rmd
The AI tab’s flow vignettes/articles/ai-flow.Rmd

Where this file and CONTRIBUTING.md disagree, tell a maintainer.

In short

  • Dependencies point one way: rtfreporter <- tflspec <- tflplanner. A change to the table layout belongs in rtfreporter, a change to the spec in tflspec: change it upstream first; tflplanner only follows.

  • Fictional data only. No company, study or patient data in code, tests, fixtures, examples, issues or pull requests, and none sent to an AI service.

  • R code is ASCII (\uXXXX escapes). Every text the app shows has its Japanese in inst/i18n/strings/<file>.csv.

  • Record the change in the PR description. A PR never edits NEWS.md, CHANGELOG.md or Version:, and there is no separate memo file. Fill the template’s User-visible change (for NEWS) field without being asked: one or two bullets in NEWS style (what a user can now do, or what is fixed, named by its function or argument), or “none” for an internal change; then “Breaking: no”, or “Breaking: yes” with the migration. The maintainers write NEWS.md from the merged PRs at release. For example:

    ## User-visible change (for NEWS)

- The AI tab's docs field adds a file at once: on Browse, on Enter, or on
  leaving the field.

Breaking: no

  • Before a pull request: the tests of what you changed and lintr on the changed files (see CONTRIBUTING.md).

  • Outside contributors open pull requests against main. The next branch, the automerge label and merge-after: lines are the maintainers’ own workflow; a maintainer adds any label that is needed.

Screens

  • Labels are “meaning (function / argument name)”, e.g. “Parameter (param: PARAMCD)”.
  • The standard screens are for expert users: cut guidance an expert would not need, or move it behind a “?”.
  • Never drop data silently. Keep what a screen cannot show as YAML, and show it.
  • Every text shown has its Japanese in inst/i18n/strings/<file>.csv (the R file that shows it; common.csv for several). test-app-robust checks this, and translation keys must be unique (a test fails on duplicates).
  • Start the app from your branch and look at the screen first, before the heavy checks. Keep a pull request to one screen.

Tests and files

  • Run tests where they are; never copy them into a temporary folder (test_file() reads that folder’s setup*.R).
  • Before loading tflplanner, point R_USER_CONFIG_DIR, R_USER_DATA_DIR, R_USER_CACHE_DIR and options(tflplanner.home =) at a scratch home, never the user’s.
  • Browser tests (test-e2e-*.R, chromote) run only with TFLPLANNER_E2E=true.
  • Run the installed package’s tests in one R session as well (test_dir): per-file runs miss interference between tests.
  • app_server()’s parts are R/srv_<part>.R (functions run in its environment by .srv_part()). Split a file once it passes 2,000 lines.

Git work for a contributor

If you are an agent working for a contributor, you do the git work as well. Their fork is origin; https://github.com/ichirio/tflplanner.git is upstream (git remote add upstream <url>, one time only). Check with git remote -v before you start. Run git status first; if the working tree has uncommitted changes, commit them or ask, and never discard them.

Update the fork’s main

Do this before every new piece of work. A fork does not update itself. Keep main pristine: never commit to it.

git checkout main
git fetch upstream
git merge --ff-only upstream/main
git push origin main

Then cut the topic branch: git checkout -b <type>/<issue>-<slug>.

If the fork’s main has gone stale or has its own commits

If git merge --ff-only fails, main has commits upstream does not have. Stop and tell the contributor which commits (git log upstream/main..main). The reset below discards them, so run it only after they agree, and keep the work on a branch first:

git branch my-old-work main
git fetch upstream
git checkout main
git reset --hard upstream/main
git push origin main --force-with-lease

This is the only time main is ever force-pushed.

Rebase a topic branch on upstream/main

Do this when the branch has fallen behind, or when CI or a reviewer asks for it.

git fetch upstream
git checkout <topic-branch>
git rebase upstream/main

If there are conflicts, git stops at each one:

  1. git status lists the conflicted files. Open each one and keep both sides’ intent: upstream’s change and the contributor’s.
  2. If you cannot tell what a side intended, read its commit (git log -p upstream/main -- <file>). If you still cannot tell, run git rebase --abort and ask. Don’t guess.
  3. git add <file>, then git rebase --continue. Repeat until it finishes. Never edit Version: or NEWS.md to settle a conflict; take upstream’s.

Then run the tests of the area you changed again, because a rebase changes the code under them. Only when they pass:

git push --force-with-lease origin <topic-branch>
  • --force-with-lease on the topic branch only: a rebase rewrites its history, so a plain push is refused.
  • Never use plain --force. If --force-with-lease is refused, someone else pushed to the branch: fetch and look at what they pushed before going on.
  • Never force-push main, except for the stale-fork reset above.

When CI or a review asks for a rebase

  • “This branch is out of date” or “has conflicts”: rebase as above and push. The pull request updates by itself; don’t open a new one, and don’t close it.
  • CI failed: read the failed step’s log first. If the failure comes from your change, fix it in a new commit on the branch. Rebase only if upstream has moved past a fix you need.
  • A review asked for changes: add commits on the branch and reply on the pull request. Don’t rewrite history that the reviewer has already read, unless they asked for a rebase or squash.
  • Stop and ask the contributor if a rebase would drop commits you didn’t write, or if conflicts reach beyond the files they changed.
